items.label: section_header
items.text: SPECIFIC HEAT CAPACITY

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: The unit for specific heat capacity is J/g/°C or J g-1°C-1.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: Again, we are using the delta (∆) symbol to indicate a change, but this time a temperature change. The concept of specific heat capacity

items.label: text
items.text: also applies to the cooling of a substance. For example, to cool 1 g of water by 1 °C we need to take out 4.18J of energy.

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection. Do not carry a lit spirit burner and do not fill or re-fill one when there is a naked flame nearby.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: A calorimeter is simply something that we do a calorimetry experiment in; here it is a copper can, in other experiments it can be a polystyrene cup.

items.label: text
items.text: When we heat something up, it gets hotter. The specific heat capacity tells us about how much energy has to be put in to increase the temperature of something. The specific heat capacity of a substance is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C.

items.label: text
items.text: For water, the value is 4.18 J/g/°C (joules per gram per degree Celsius). This means that 4.18J of heat energy is needed if we want to increase the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C. If you want the temperature of 1 g of water to go up by 2 °C, then 4.18 × 2 = 8.36 J of heat energy must be supplied. If now you have 2 g of water, then 2 × 8.36 J of energy would be needed to raise the temperature by 2 °C.

items.label: text
items.text: The amount of heat energy required is directly proportional to the mass (m) and the temperature change (∆T) of the substance. The following equation can be           l   the temperature of mass m by ∆T°C:

items.label: text
items.text: heat energy change = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change Q=m×c×∆T

items.label: section_header
items.text: CALORIMETRY EXPERIMENTS FOR DETERMINING THE ENTHALPY CHANGES OF REACTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: It is fairly uncomplicated to measure the amount of heat absorbed or given out in several kinds of chemical reactions and physical changes. The technique used to do this is called calorimetry and it is based on the idea that if we use the heat from a reaction to heat another substance, such as water, we can then use the equation introduced above (Q = mc∆T) to calculate the amount of heat released. Here the mass, the specific heat capacity and the temperature change are all referring to the substance heated. If we know how many moles of reactants are used in the reaction, we can then work out the molar enthalpy change, ∆H, of the reaction in theunit kJ/mol.

items.label: text
items.text: The following activity illustrates how we can use calorimetry to determine the molar enthalpy change of combustion of an alcohol, i.e. how much heat energy is released when 1 mole of alcohol burns.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACTIVITY 1

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: MEASURING ENTHALPY CHANGES IN COMBUSTION REACTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: One of the most common calorimetry experiments at International GCSE is to measure the amount of heat given off when a number of small alcohols are burned. You could use methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol (see Chapter 22 for an introduction to the naming of alcohols).

items.label: text
items.text: The alcohols are burned in a small spirit burner, and the heat produced is used to heat some water in a copper can (the calorimeter).

items.label: text
items.text: The following procedure could be used:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Measure 100 cm³ of cold water using a measuring cylinder and transfer the water to a copper can.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Take the initial temperature of the water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Weigh a spirit-burner containing ethanol with its lid on. The lid should be kept on when the wick is not lit to prevent the alcohol from evaporating.
